content: 1. The administration of vitamin K to mothers prior to preterm delivery did not demonstrate a significant improvement in outcomes for preterm infants, as reported by Crowther in 2010. 2. Veldman (2006) investigated the use of recombinant activated Factor VII (FVIIa) in the context of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) development, but the study was limited by a small sample size. 3. Plasma transfusion is often administered prophylactically to preterm infants who are at risk due to abnormal coagulation studies or early signs of disease, with the belief that it may prevent bleeding or normalize coagulation. 4. In a recent study by Motta (2014), 63% of plasma transfusions were given prophylactically to infants without any bleeding episodes. 5. Stanworth (2011) reported that 58% of plasma transfusion episodes were based on abnormal coagulation studies without clinical bleeding, and an additional 14% involved prophylactic plasma transfusion without prior coagulation testing. 6. Preventing the progression of existing IVH was cited as an indication for plasma transfusion in 18.6% of cases, according to Motta (2014). 7. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) by Beverley (1985) involving infants born at less than 32 weeks of gestation or weighing less than 1500 grams found that plasma transfusion reduced the incidence of IVH. 8. A more recent study by Dani (2009) showed a non-significant reduction in the relative risk of IVH in infants who received plasma transfusion in response to abnormal coagulation tests without evidence of bleeding, compared to those who received transfusion after a bleeding event. 9. This Cochrane Review aims to evaluate the role of plasma transfusion in preventing IVH among very preterm neonates, who are prone to severe intraventricular bleeding and exhibit prolonged coagulation times in laboratory tests. 10. Plasma products, such as fresh frozen plasma (FFP), contain plasma proteins, including procoagulant and inhibitory components of the coagulation cascade, acute phase proteins, immunoglobulins, complement, transport molecules, and albumin. 11. Many coagulation factors have short half-lives; for example, Factor VII has a half-life of three to five hours, leaving minimal amounts in circulation after eight hours. 12. Plasma products are primarily derived from whole blood, although they can also be obtained through plasmapheresis. 13. The timing of freezing after collection determines whether the product is classified as FFP (frozen within six to eight hours) or F24 (frozen within 24 hours). 14. Both FFP and F24 can be stored at temperatures of −18°C or colder, with F24 having slightly lower levels of Factor VIII and Factor V compared to FFP. 15. The term frozen plasma encompasses both FFP and F24 products. 16. Variability among transfused plasma units is less pronounced in pooled plasma components, such as solvent detergent-treated frozen plasma. 17. Solvent detergent-treated frozen plasma is prepared from pools of 300 to 5000 plasma donations and is one of the pathogen-inactivated plasma preparations available for clinical use. 18. Pathogen inactivation technology provides an additional safety measure to reduce the risk of transfusion-transmitted infections. 19. Common pathogen inactivation methods for plasma include solvent detergent treatment, methylene blue treatment (using a phenothiazine dye and light), and amotosalen treatment (using psoralens and ultraviolet A light). 20. While these methods offer effective viral protection and reduce microbial infectivity, they may alter or reduce the content of coagulation factors. 21. Frozen plasma is typically administered in doses of 10 mL/kg, though doses can range up to 20 mL/kg. These volumes may impact hemodynamic status and fluid balance in preterm infants. 22. Plasma transfusions carry risks of adverse reactions and infections, including potential exposure to unidentified pathogens. 23. Preventing or treating IVH early could improve long-term survival without disability in very preterm infants. 24. Currently, there is no treatment available for IVH once it occurs, and most strategies focus on prevention or addressing underlying risk factors (McCrea, 2008). 25. Very low birth weight infants are known to have prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) compared to term infants and adults. 26. Plasma transfusions, containing both procoagulant and anticoagulant components, are used in adult, pediatric, and neonatal patients to correct coagulopathy in those who are bleeding or at risk of bleeding (Stanworth, 2011). 27. Defects in hemostasis have been associated with the occurrence of IVH (Beverley, 1984). 28. Plasma administration may reduce bleeding tendencies in preterm infants with prolonged coagulation times, potentially preventing the occurrence or progression of low-grade IVH into more severe forms (Grades III and IV, Papile, 1978). 29. The effects of frozen plasma may not solely result from improved coagulation factor concentrations but could involve other mechanisms. 30. Associations between unstable blood pressure, variable cerebral blood flow, and IVH have been well-documented (Ballah, 2010; Perlman, 1983; Van Bel, 1987). 31. Plasma transfusion may stabilize hemodynamic circulation, preventing rapid blood pressure changes and subsequent fluctuations in cerebral blood flow. 32. If this is the mechanism, other fluids might achieve similar effects without the risks associated with transfusion reactions. 33. Fresh frozen plasma transfusion likely acts through two mechanisms: correcting coagulopathy and preventing fluctuations in blood pressure, thereby stabilizing cerebral blood flow in pressure-passive cerebral circulation. 34. Through these mechanisms, FFP may prevent the development or progression of new hemorrhages (Fanaroff, 2006; Julkunen, 2008; Salonvaara, 2005). 35. IVH most commonly occurs within the first 72 hours of life, a period when infants are most unstable and at greatest risk. 36. Infants will be included in this Cochrane Review only if plasma is administered within the first 24 hours of life. 37. Severe IVH is a major cause of significant disability in preterm infants. 38. Up to 50% of survivors with Grade III IVH and up to 75% of those with Grade IV IVH experience definitive neurological sequelae (Volpe, 2008). 39. The aim of this review is to determine the efficacy of plasma transfusion in preventing IVH and to provide clinicians with robust evidence to guide clinical decisions. 40. This is the first systematic review conducted on this topic. 41. Despite the perceived benefits of frozen plasma in preventing IVH, the actual benefit of this practice has not been clearly demonstrated. 42. Plasma transfusion carries potential risks, including volume overload, infection, and transfusion reactions. 43. A careful evaluation of the potential benefits of frozen plasma in relation to its safety profile, dosing, route, and duration of administration is necessary. 44. It remains unclear whether prophylactic administration of frozen plasma prevents neonatal IVH in all high-risk groups.
